utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-98-30/1-A, The Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Mladjo Radic, Zoran Zigic, and Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Anthony Carmona. Appearing with me on behalf of the Prosecution is Ms. Norul Rashid, and our case manager is Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kvocka, we have a message here from your counsel, Mr. Simic, saying that he has been unable to get his Visa. Apparently he put his application in too late. And although the Registry offered him some speedy service, he didn't respond. But he has said he doesn't wish to raise any issue. Do you understand that? THE APPELLANT KVOCKA: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have received the same information. And in the interests of efficiency, I have no objection that we work in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Toma Fila, and I am Defence counsel for the accused Mladjo Radic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am Slobodan Stojanovic, attorney from Belgrade. And I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And for Mr. Prcac. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Attorney Jovan Simic representing Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, you had a great victory over the Registry in relation to your fax machine. You got a copy of the report, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. I'm afraid I still haven't finished my job. I see that there are a number of remarks regarding our lines in Belgrade, but I must inform the Court that I have the best provider in Belgrade, and I think we will have to ask for assistance to improve our lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you might, and perhaps all counsel from Belgrade, should note this: As a result of this investigation that was carried out because of the troubles Mr. Stojanovic had, or at least the Registry had with Mr. Stojanovic and his fax machine, the Registry has set up KPN lines, the Dutch provider, which are very much more expensive, I gather, than the ones they usually use. But because they get better results with KPN, they are going to use KPN for all calls to Belgrade. But there are problems, according to the investigation, with the quality of the lines once they get to Belgrade. And the people in the Registry who did this investigation have said it is impossible to get through if you have an answering machine connected. And that it would be better if you had a dedicated fax line, that you didn't use it for any other purpose, and that the facsimile machine should be set on auto answering. With all of those things, one hopes that they will do better in getting through. But Mr. Stojanovic, there's still a problem, on the 23rd of May, they attempted twice to send you a letter from the senior legal officer. They attempted again on the 26th of May. And at that stage, they gave up. And they are using KPN lines, by the way. They gave up, and they sent it to you by registered post. Now, according to the registered post system, there should be a receipt that you should sign when you receive it. But they haven't got that receipt back yet. Did you get a letter from the senior legal officer dated the 23rd of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did receive it on the 9th of June. It was a holiday here in Holland. And on that same day, half an hour later, I sent an email that I certainly accept what the legal officer suggested, and I considered it to be very useful for the Defence. That is why hard copy was received also on the 10th of June of this communication of mine. But that was just an announcement as to what I would do. Indeed, today, I filed a confidential addendum to Zoran Zigic's motion filed on the 22nd of August last year, so the first submission pursuant to Rule 115 was filed by me today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you sign a receipt for the letter? I think we better get our procedure sorted out. Was there a receipt there for you to sign when the letter was delivered to you by post?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, Your Honour. I think this is a rule that the post office does not always apply, but this time I'm quite sure that I did sign it. It was on the 9th of June, maybe around 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's only four days later, and we'll eventually receive it. But you realise that you had not dealt with the issue of due diligence, which is one you must establish, that even though the evidence may not have been immediately available to you, it could not have been discovered through the exercise of due diligence. There is also a problem that in your first motion, you had not produced the material you wanted tendered itself. You had only given us your version of what you thought that it meant. But we've got to have the actual material itself. Have you repaired that omission?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just referring to that material that is linked to our first motion, and that was filed today. I think that I have fully implemented your suggestions today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How about the due diligence point? Have you demonstrated -- it doesn't appear from the document itself very readily anyway - that this material could not have been discovered through the exercise of due diligence on your part during the course of the trial? Do you realise that that is what you must establish?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we did provide a response in our submissions to that question. To what extent that will be acceptable, it is up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't want to argue it here. I just wanted to be sure that you understood you had to do that in order to have this application under Rule 115 considered. If you say you have, well, I accept that, and we'll see what you have produced. Are there any other matters that you wish to raise while you're on your feet?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing that I could say is that it seems to me that a ruling is missing on the part of the pre-Appeals Judge regarding a question that we raised in reference to errors in the transcript and the judgement, namely on the 7th of March, 2002, you made a ruling regarding that matter. The Prosecution and the Defence did achieve some agreement and informed the Chamber about it, that there were certain errors in the transcript. But it is not just an error in the transcript, but it is literally quoted in the judgement. And regarding the wording of your ruling that I mentioned, of the 7th of March, 2002, it seems to me that a decision on the part of the Chamber is required prior to the actual appeals hearing. That is, the parties have established that there was an error in the transcript, and that transcript was erroneously quoted in the judgement. That is paragraph 584 of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I haven't got a copy of what was said on the 7th of March, but I am doubtful that I would have said that is a matter for me to decide. I don't know why you say that I haven't decided it. That is sort of thing that will be dealt with at the hearing, in my view. If there's a measure of agreement, then it will be taken as having been noted that there was an error in the transcript which found its way into the judgement. I don't see that you need anything more than that, if that's what has been agreed. But I'm afraid, there has been a lot of water under the bridge in the 15 months since then, apart from the fact that we have about four appeals all starting with the letter K, which I managed to get sometimes hopelessly confused in my mind when I'm dealing with these pre-appeal matters. But if you feel that there has been some omission on the part of the Appeals Chamber to decide it, then I suggest you put in a document saying so, and we'll go back and we'll have a look. What was happening on the 7th of March? Was that a Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a decision of yours. I could just read a paragraph from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "Considering that where the parties are in agreement that the transcript of the proceedings contains errors, there is no bar to having those amendments made to the transcript prior to the hearing of the appeal by the Appeals Chamber." [Interpretation] I would like to point out. It's not just an error in the transcript, but also an error in the judgement because that same quote was copied literally in paragraph 584. And in a sense, it is an introduction to Zigic's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you've said that three times, and I'm sure you will be saying it again. But my point is this: If that has been said, then there is an agreement between the parties that the transcript was wrong. That's as far as we can take it. The transcript that we are supplied with is called an uncorrected version. I've never seen a corrected version. But nevertheless, everybody will know, and you will have in your submissions, I assume, a reference to the fact that the transcript has been agreed to be wrong, and that the Trial Chamber has incorporated that error in its judgement. Now, I don't think there's anything more that can be done at this stage. But the appeal will proceed upon that understanding. Now, is there anything more you want to add to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We just felt that it wasn't purely up to the parties to determine what the transcript should be like. We feel that the Chamber is the meritorious body. It is after all -- the transcript is a document of the Chamber, and we felt that the Chamber should decide. And I had the impression that a prior decision was needed. But I don't feel that that is absolutely essential and that it could not be dealt with together when the entire appeal is heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, for the years that I sat on the Trial Chamber here, I used to read the transcript every day to check that at least what I had said or what was said to me was correctly recorded. And every day, I put in a list of what I saw to be corrections. Now, they are probably somewhere in a file. But I have never seen a corrected version of the transcript. So just don't worry about it. That's what happens, I'm afraid, in this place. You will be protected at the hearing. Now, is there anything else you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Fila, have you got anything that you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, we have received a submission yesterday, a motion, in which the Prosecution is asking to disclose to us some new material by the end of June. And we are concerned by the duration of these proceedings and how long will this disclosure of materials continue? It's not something that only I personally am concerned by, because it is not me that is in question but the person for whom I am Defence counsel, and who, of course, is interested in having a speedy solution because in my view, a fair trial implies a speedy trial. And I had a discussion on that subject with Mr. Cassesse in his day. So what I am worried about, and this is something that I referred to the last time, if Mr. Zigic's trial should be separated from us, I would be in favour because we really don't believe that we can receive anything that would be useful to us. I don't like to use strong words in life generally, but I fear that this will never stop. We keep -- we will keep on receiving unnecessary documents. Then I sit around reading them, and of course as I say, it's not that I'm wasting time. That doesn't matter. And then if I say that something is important out of those materials, I'm told by the Prosecution that it isn't. First I'm told it is significant, then I'm told it isn't. So I have a feeling that somebody is playing a game with me and my time, and the time of the Chamber. If I were to do that, I would have been found in contempt at least three times by now, if I were to say that time and again. And I'm sorry for using your time to say this. Either there should be a severing of the case, because we're no longer interested in these unnecessary documents from the Prosecution. So to wind up, the only way to put an end to this is to fix a date when we will have the appeals hearing and when these materials will stop being disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you have been around this Tribunal for a very long time, and I'm sure this has been said to you before. But the fact that the Prosecution provides you with material under Rule 68 is not a concession by them that it will exculpate your client. What they say is: "Here is material which is capable of being exculpatory," so there's no games in it. They are, perhaps, erring on the side of caution. I don't know. If you find that the material they supply to you is not exculpatory, then that's that. They don't want to be accused, I should think, of having failed to supply something which you suddenly see to be exculpatory which they may have had a doubt about. That's all they're doing. The problem with the Prosecution's approach, and I'm not trying to criticise anybody in particular, but they constantly go along to the duty judge with an application for a warrant to seize material. It's not just in relation to this case. Some reason upstairs there, they don't understand that everybody is trying to close this Tribunal down, and they are still investigating other cases. And by doing the investigations, and they seize documents, they have an obligation, and this has been made very Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clear to them in a number of cases, they have an obligation to check that material to see if any of it is capable of being exculpatory in relation to any of the matters which have been through the Tribunal. So that's why it constantly comes. At the time that the case and the appeal is listed for hearing, then they no doubt will still continue to send it to you even after the appeal is over. But you need not concern -- we are not waiting until they finish in order to list the case. The problem is, of course, the applications for fresh evidence. So that's why that's happening. Now, Mr. Simic, is there anything that you want to raise? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have nothing new to state, except for saying that we would express our concern over the prolongation which seems to us not by chance, but intentional. And that if we continue in this way, then we might be here during the time that we're pensioned off, if the Prosecution persists. So we would like to have scheduled our oral arguments or to know when the Prosecution will fulfill its duties. And it should have fulfilled that duty a long time ago. Let us not forget the part of the documents were in their possession before the end of trial, so all we would like to say is we would like to know when this is going to be for our defendants, the people that have been accused, and who are waiting to hear their sentence or culpability being established or not established. Thank you -- pronounced guilty or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I am very grateful that it's not my task to fix dates for hearings; it's the President's tasks. It's not an easy one, and he is certainly pressing to get this end two other appeals, which have been sitting here for some time bogged down with Rule 115 matters. He's very anxious to get them on. So you will get the earliest possible hearing date. Now, Mr. Carmona, I'm sorry that the Prosecution has been left last this time, but nevertheless are there any matters you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Certainly, in fact, Your Honours. In relation to the whole issue with regard to separation of this appeal, the Prosecution is of the view that the exigency of justice and the particular circumstances of this case would, in fact, initiate -- or to initiate, in fact, a hearing together. And in fact we do not think, for example, that the ends of justice would be met by any separation of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is no motion on for a separation any longer. There was one at the time when Mr. Zigic and Mr. Stojanovic parted company, but that was rejected because to start with, Mr. Stojanovic came back into the fold, and the matter is proceeding somewhat fitfully, but they are all running together.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honours, I wish to in fact categorically disabuse my friends' minds with regard to in fact any kind of delay on the part of the Prosecution. We are as anxious to expedite this matter. We do appreciate, for example, the fact that this particular Tribunal is a type of judicial animal that has a life-span. And we certainly in fact want this matter expedited. But each particular case has its particular idiosyncrasy, and in these circumstances you will appreciate, Your Honours, that we have had cases, for example, that are going on presently. Cases that, in fact, have in fact since completed, like Stakic; cases in fact in fortuna, like Meakic; and cases as I said in fact that are in fact in the process, like Gruban, where, in fact, material is, in fact, being generated time and time again. And as much as, in fact, for example, the Prosecution's responsibility may appear to be onerous, sometimes burdensome, sometime weary legged, we do have a responsibility to get these particular documents and material and determine whether, in fact, there is anything that can assist the Defence. And Your Honours, I remember very categorically, in the second Status Conference, you had, in fact, told counsel in no uncertain terms on -- in fact, on the Friday, the 14th Status Conference, at page 51, you said essentially that our obligation to produce material which may prove to be exculpatory. The Prosecution does not by mention in these documents admit that they are in fact exculpatory. Secondly, Your Honours have indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Carmona, I'm sorry to interrupt. But I've said all that already. You don't have to tell me. I've pointed that out to the accuseds' counsel myself. You don't have to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm indeed grateful to the observation of Your Honour. In any event, Your Honours, the bottom line is, in fact, we have, in fact, attempted to accelerate this entire process. And I can say now that only, in fact, this morning I got assurance from, in fact, the ISU, that they are, in fact, as much as, in fact, the report indicated that they would complete the process by the end of next week or end of next week. They indicated very categorically that they are in a position to complete the process but Tuesday of next week. We, in fact, are not saying by any stretch of the imagination that the process would finish at the end of the month. We are saying, in fact, that at maximum it would finish at the end of the month. But we are hoping, in fact, to finish the entire process by at least a week before the end of the month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Carmona, having put forward your policy statement, may I repeat what I have said on several earlier occasions, somebody in the Prosecution, and you can guess who, has to do something about the sharing of resources there. That we are now in a stage where this Tribunal is in its exit strategy, I think is the buzzword, and that all of these teams that keep on investigating new cases should be put to work helping to run the current ones. And I'm talking particularly about the Rule 68 obligations to search this material for exculpatory matter. We have been told so often by the Prosecution that you have limited resources to do it. The time has come for somebody in the Prosecution office to do something about that and to move some of the huge resources you have back into running these trials, rather than chasing other criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And we have this problem every time that the question of Rule 68 and exculpatory material arises, we get a plea from the Prosecution: "We do not have the resources to do more than one case at a time." Well, I've said it before and I'll say it again: That's not good enough. I've had my say. Do you want to say anything in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, it is not my intention to indicate policy here, but I can tell you, in fact, from my -- our prospective in the Kvocka team, we, in fact, are making great attempts to ameliorate the situation by attempting to get individuals to work extra hours. I can tell you, in fact, in relation to this particular matter, there were some people down at the beach, but they are in a beach house, doing searches on Monday during the holidays. And as a result, we are in a position to say in relation to this particular matter that we can complete the exercise before the end of this month. You know, and this is essentially, in fact, our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Carmona, I'm not criticising the team. I'm criticising the system. The systemic failure to provide sufficient resources particularly in relation to exculpatory material which must be provided under Rule 68. Another problem that I see, as a pre-Appeal Judge, a continuing series of pleas by the Prosecution for extra time to do things because you have so much work on your hands. Now, again, I don't criticise the particular teams in the Appeals Chamber section of the OTP. I believe you all try your best. But the time has come for somebody to move some greater resources into that section so that you can keep up. And I think that the Prosecution is going to find that that plea will fall on very deaf ears, but that's the only way we can get these matters on. So there must be some consideration given by somebody in the Office of the Prosecutor to moving some resources from where they are now not really necessary to where they really are desperately needed. Now, that's as far as I'll take it. Do you want to say anything in support of this application for an extension of pages in the last filing by the Prosecution? You signed it, I notice, on behalf of Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm a bit puzzled with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's an application for an extension of four pages to the further response that you were given leave to file.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I point out to you at least two things in relation to the documents being filed: First, despite all the warnings about not trying to have the last say on matters which you do not have a right to have a last say on, there is at least a page and a half of this document which deals precisely with a matter that you had no right to address on. The second thing is, and the application for the extension of pages is directed to the second issue that you were given leave to respond further on, the one about the admissibility of prior consistent statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is very clear from what I said in that decision that the assistance we sought from you was not to tell us what is and what is not admissible as a prior consistent statement. You've got to accept that some of us had some experience with these sorts of things before. What we wanted to know from you was what your attitude was as to whether any situation arose during the course of the trial which would have warranted the admission of such a document, such as recent -- an allegation of recent invention. And there's not a word about that anywhere in this long document. So you've squandered, if I may say, the space you've got. There are, in fact, two paragraphs that are in identical terms which takes about half a page. And my present inclination is to refuse the application and make you do what you're meant to do. Now, is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were of the view that the particular -- the particular decision was such that warranted, in fact, a response with regard to the rule of previous consistent statements in the context of what kind of weight would need to be attached to that particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You had the feeling, did you, that that's what we needed assistance on, that we didn't know that when a prior consistent statement was admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: We were of the view, also, that, in fact, a particular trial never, in fact, arose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why didn't you say so. There's not one word of that. And that's the assistance we wanted. You are the people who at this stage are far more familiar with the issues that arose at the trial than any of us is. And what we will have to do is to get our legal officers to read through the whole of the trial, to find whether that issue arose, because you have given us no assistance. Neither, of course, has the appellant, and I accept that. But the Prosecution has got a duty to assist as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that's the assistance that I gave you the right to file a new document about. And you haven't done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem with the particular -- this particular, in fact, decision is that, in fact, it actually came into our possession late on Friday afternoon, and, in fact, we weren't able to look at it from Tuesday, so we were indeed pressed for time in an attempt to meet the deadlines, we had to, in fact, respond quickly and expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Don't you think it might have been a good idea, and I'm sorry to interrupt you, and I'm sorry to the interpreters for doing so, but don't you think it might have been a good idea to have read it before you had rushed off and poured over some old textbooks to give us something which I'm sure every lawyer in this building would know?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact at paragraph 43 of that particular response, in fact, we did state our position with regard, in fact, to that particular piece of evidence. And I refer, specifically, to, in fact, the last four lines of that particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, that's all you had to say. If you think that's a sufficient answer, that's all you had to say. I'm afraid somebody is going to have to sit down and do a document that fits in within the limit because I think probably, there's a certain degree of irritation in my voice, and you may be assured I was irritated when I sat down and started reading a page and a half of material that you were not entitled to even raise. Even after I had said in the previous decision "you must not try always to get the last word on something that you're not entitled to have the last word on."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if, in fact, the Court is minded, and in an attempt to assist the Court, we are, in fact, prepared, if, in fact, we are allowed, to possibly, in fact, respond by filing an addendum to this particular document within a particular short time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You don't get out of page references by just putting in two or three documents, each of which fills out the page limit, so you get three times the page limit. What I'm saying is you've got to use a little bit of discipline to answer something --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- within the limit. You realise, don't you, that the previous document you had filed in which you had set out what your reply was you dealt with five issues in a little over two pages. Now, I limited you to two issues, and you've taken 14 pages to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if, in fact, you could assist us in this regard. But to indicate which of those pages, in fact, you're referring to particularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Paragraphs 4 to 6 are irrelevant. Paragraph 10 is a complete repetition. That makes up a page and a half, to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, in fact, this is the particular pages of contention you're referring to, particularly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Those are the ones that are irrelevant. What I'm saying is that you seek the additional pages because you say you wanted to spend a lot of time on the second issue. And if that sentence that you've referred to is your answer which is the only assistance you're going to give us, then you could have said that in four lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: But certainly, Your Honours, it is our intention, in fact, to assist this Court in a proper determination of the issues. And if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You certainly weren't assisting us the last time. I'm not blaming you, but I spent a lot of time on that last motion because the Prosecution had failed completely to give us any assistance as to why it should get a right of response. And then I get a second one like this which does not appear on the face of it to give us assistance except perhaps for those four lines. So you can see why there's a certain irritation involved. It is not, if I may say so, they type of assistance to which we have become accustomed from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the circumstances, if, in fact, the Court is minded with leave of the Court, if it is possible, in fact, that we can possibly refile a more concise document consistent with, in fact, your concerns, and in an attempt to assist this Court, we certainly would like a period of time in which to respond, because as I said on the last occasion, just a while ago, Your Honours, in fact, it was, in fact, a very pressing response in the context of the holiday period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Carmona, I know it was Whit Monday. It's a holiday I'm not used to having. I must confess it's very nice to be in Europe to get these extra holidays. But nevertheless, bearing in mind that you were being given leave to file another document in order to remove the irrelevant material from the first and to expand by assisting us on this second issue, the fact that you did neither of those seems to me that it should not have taken you very long at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, you will appreciate that in relation to this particular paragraph, we did, in fact, refer in the footnote to pieces of the evidence that, in fact, supported our position. But be that as it may, Your Honour, I think, in fact, if Your Honour is minded, and, in fact, we seek leave in this regard to, possibly, in fact, file a more concise document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Next Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. Well, then, the leave that you seek will be refused, and I'll give you until Thursday to put in a document that does comply with the practice direction. And would you tell those who are responsible for this that we do really need more assistance than we're getting. Is there anything else to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Right. I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll adjourn.
